questions.stem: How many shared pairs does a molecule of nitrogen, N2, contain?

options.explanation: Nitrogen shares three pairs between its two atoms, the largest count among the common diatomic molecules.
One pair would suit hydrogen or chlorine; nitrogen needs three pairs to complete both outer shells.
Two pairs belong to oxygen's double bond; nitrogen shares one pair more.
Five pairs is beyond any molecule in this course; nitrogen shares exactly three.

questions.stem: In the dot-and-cross diagram for hydrogen chloride, what is shared?

options.text: One electron pair, one electron from the hydrogen and one from the chlorine
options.explanation: The single bond of HCl is one shared pair with one donor electron from each atom.

options.text: A pair of electrons both donated by the chlorine
options.explanation: Each atom contributes one electron to a normal covalent bond; neither atom donates the whole pair.

options.text: All seven of chlorine's outer electrons
options.explanation: Only one of chlorine's outer electrons enters the bond; the other six stay non-bonding.
Hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so they bond covalently by sharing.

questions.stem: How many electrons are shared in total in a molecule of oxygen, O2?

options.text: Four, because oxygen forms two covalent bonds and each bond carries one shared pair
options.explanation: Two shared pairs means four shared electrons in total across the double bond.

options.text: Two, one from each atom into a single pair
options.explanation: Two shared electrons would be one single bond; oxygen shares two pairs.

options.text: Sixteen, all of the electrons present
options.explanation: Only the four bonding electrons are shared; the remaining electrons stay non-bonding on their own atoms.
Eight would be four pairs; the oxygen molecule carries exactly two shared pairs.

questions.stem: Which diatomic molecules are named in the spec for this diagram skill?

options.text: Hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, the halogens and the hydrogen halides
options.explanation: The spec lists these diatomic families for dot-and-cross practice, alongside the named inorganic and organic molecules.
The halogens are one family on the list; hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and the hydrogen halides are named too.

options.text: All diatomic molecules in the Periodic Table
options.explanation: The requirement covers the named families, not every diatomic possibility.
The full list runs from hydrogen through nitrogen, the halogens and the hydrogen halides.

questions.stem: What does one covalent bond always represent?

options.explanation: The exam hint states it directly: each covalent bond is one shared pair, whatever the molecule.
Two pairs make a double bond, which is a specific case such as oxygen, not the general bond.
Transfer belongs to ionic bonding; covalent bonds share a pair.
The equivalence is fixed: one bond, one pair, two electrons.

questions.stem: Define a diatomic molecule and list the diatomic substances named in the note.
questions.modelAnswer: A diatomic molecule contains exactly two atoms; the note names H2, Cl2, O2, N2 and HCl.

questions.stem: State how many shared pairs the bonds in oxygen and in nitrogen contain, and what bond name each earns.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen shares two pairs, giving a double bond, and nitrogen shares three pairs, giving a triple bond.

questions.stem: Explain why each shared pair in a dot-and-cross drawing is drawn with one electron shown as a dot and one as a cross.
questions.modelAnswer: Each shared pair in the drawing uses one electron from each atom, and keeping the donor symbols visible shows exactly which atom supplied each electron of the pair.

questions.stem: A student draws a dot-and-cross diagram for fluorine, F2, showing four shared electrons between the two atoms. Using the halogen bonding pattern of record, correct the drawing.
questions.modelAnswer: Like the other halogens, fluorine forms a single covalent bond, so only one pair is shared in F2; the drawing should show exactly two shared electrons, one from each atom.

questions.stem: How many covalent bonds does one molecule of ammonia, NH3, contain?

options.text: Three, one between the nitrogen and each hydrogen
options.explanation: Each N-H link is one shared pair, and the molecule carries three of them.
One bond would join nitrogen to a single hydrogen; the formula NH3 names three hydrogens.
Four bonds would suit methane's carbon; ammonia's nitrogen bonds to three hydrogens.
Two bonds would leave one hydrogen unattached; the three hydrogens each need a bond.

questions.stem: What is the bonding in carbon dioxide, CO2?

options.text: Two double bonds, one between the carbon and each oxygen atom
options.explanation: Carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen, and the two oxygens are otherwise unconnected.
Single bonds would leave carbon two pairs short of its four-bond pattern.

options.text: One double bond between the two oxygen atoms
options.explanation: The oxygens bond to the carbon, not to each other; carbon sits at the centre.

options.text: A triple bond and a single bond
options.explanation: The pattern at this level is two identical double bonds; mixed bond orders do not appear here.

questions.stem: Which organic molecules must you be able to draw dot-and-cross diagrams for?

options.text: Methane, ethane, ethene, and organic molecules containing halogen atoms, up to two carbons
options.explanation: The spec caps the organic list at two carbon atoms and includes the halogen-substituted versions.
Longer chains sit beyond the stated cap of two carbon atoms.
Methane is the smallest example; ethane, ethene and halogenated molecules are named too.
Rings with more than two carbons fall outside the two-carbon cap.

questions.stem: How many shared pairs surround the carbon atom in methane, CH4?

options.text: Four, one pair with each hydrogen
options.explanation: Carbon's four bonding pairs are each shared with one hydrogen, completing every outer shell.
Two pairs would leave two of carbon's four bonds unformed.
Eight pairs would mean sixteen shared electrons; methane carries four pairs.

options.text: None, the hydrogens bond to each other
options.explanation: The four hydrogens each bond to the central carbon, not to one another.

questions.stem: Ethene, C2H4, contains a carbon-carbon double bond. What does that mean for the shared electrons?

options.text: Two pairs, four electrons, are shared between the two carbon atoms
options.explanation: A double bond is two shared pairs, so four electrons join the carbons.
One pair makes a single bond, as in ethane; ethene's carbon link is double.
Three pairs would be a triple bond, which belongs to nitrogen among the named molecules.
Four pairs exceed any bond in this course; a double bond carries exactly two.

questions.stem: Describe the bonding pattern of carbon dioxide in a dot-and-cross diagram.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide shares two pairs with each oxygen atom, making two double bonds in the molecule.

questions.stem: State how many C-H single bonds methane has and what extra bond ethane adds between its carbons.
questions.modelAnswer: Methane has four single C-H bonds, and ethane adds a C-C single bond between its two carbon atoms.

questions.stem: Explain what the formula C2H4 tells you about the bonding between ethene's two carbon atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethene contains a C=C double bond: two shared pairs sit between its two carbon atoms, so the carbons are joined by two covalent bonds at once.

questions.stem: A student must draw a dot-and-cross diagram for chloromethane, CH3Cl. Using the organic-molecules-in-scope rule of record, state what the diagram must contain.
questions.modelAnswer: Chloromethane is in scope because organic molecules in this skill contain up to two carbon atoms, including versions with halogen atoms attached; the diagram shows four single bonds from the carbon — three C-H bonds and one C-Cl bond — with every outer electron drawn.
